lesson.title: Media Access Control: Deciding Who Gets to Talk
lesson.summary: The Media Access Control sublayer of the data link layer governs how multiple devices sharing one physical medium decide when each is allowed to transmit, so that their signals do not collide and destroy each other.
lesson.body:
A point to point link connecting exactly two devices never has to answer the question of who gets to send next, since only one device is ever attached at each end. Many real networks are not like that: classic Ethernet ran over a shared coaxial cable, Wi-Fi devices share the same radio spectrum, and even a shared hub based LAN puts several stations on what is electrically one wire. Whenever more than one device can transmit onto the same medium at the same time, something has to arbitrate access, or two signals will overlap and both become unreadable. That arbitration is the job of the Media Access Control sublayer, the lower half of the data link layer, sitting just above the physical layer.

MAC is a sublayer specifically because the data link layer's job splits naturally into two concerns that do not need to know much about each other. The upper half, logical link control, deals with framing, addressing frames to a MAC address, and error detection, largely independent of what kind of shared medium is underneath. The lower half, media access control, deals purely with the scheduling problem: when is it this device's turn. That scheduling problem looks completely different depending on the medium. A wired bus, a wireless channel, and a ring topology each call for different access disciplines even though they all sit under the same logical link control.

The core resource MAC protocols allocate is transmission time on a shared channel, and every MAC scheme is ultimately a policy for answering two questions: how does a station decide it is allowed to start sending, and what happens when two stations both decide to send at once anyway. Different families of protocols answer this differently. Random access protocols, such as ALOHA and CSMA, let any station transmit whenever it has data and then deal with collisions after the fact, by detecting and retransmitting. Controlled access protocols, such as token passing, avoid collisions altogether by giving stations an explicit, orderly turn.

The MAC sublayer is also where the MAC address earns its purpose within this specific layer: a frame's destination MAC address is how a receiving station, one of potentially many listening to the same shared medium, recognizes that a given frame is addressed to it and not to a neighbor also on the same cable or radio channel. Without a MAC address to filter on, every station sharing the medium would have to hand every frame up to software just to find out it was not meant for them.

The chapters that follow this one work through the specific access disciplines that live inside the MAC sublayer: ALOHA's simplest random access scheme, carrier sense multiple access and its collision detection and collision avoidance variants, and token passing's collision free alternative. Each one is a different answer to the same underlying MAC question, how to let several devices share one medium fairly and efficiently, and each makes a different tradeoff between simplicity, efficiency under load, and the physical characteristics of the medium it was designed for.
